events.title: Lazarillo de Tormes and the picaresque
events.truthDescription: The anonymous Lazarillo de Tormes made a low-born survivor, not a perfect knight, the center of a sharp first-person story. Britannica identifies it as the original picaresque novel.
events.dareDescription: For Don Quixote, this new realism is the rival genre waiting in the road: hunger, tricks, servants, and survival keep interrupting heroic language.
events.significance: Sancho's appetite, bargaining, and earthy speech help Cervantes put chivalric fantasy into conversation with picaresque realism.

events.title: Philip II and Counter-Reformation Spain
events.truthDescription: Philip II's reign intensified Spain's role as a Catholic imperial power. Religious policing, censorship, and war shaped the atmosphere in which books could be admired, feared, regulated, and burned.
events.dareDescription: From a heroic view, Spain imagined itself as defender of the faith, a stage large enough for crusading language and knightly postures.
events.significance: The library scrutiny in Part I, Chapter 6 turns religious and political habits of censorship into a comic literary trial.

events.title: The Battle of Lepanto
events.truthDescription: Cervantes fought at Lepanto on October 7, 1571. Britannica notes that he received two gunshot wounds in the chest and a third that left his left hand useless.
events.dareDescription: Lepanto could be remembered as heroic Christian combat against Ottoman power, the kind of glory Don Quixote believes still structures the world.
events.significance: Cervantes knew real battle wounds. That experience gives special force to the novel's comedy of imagined combat and actual pain.

events.title: The Spanish Armada fails
events.truthDescription: The Armada sent by Philip II to invade England failed in 1588. Britannica describes the campaign as a failed Spanish enterprise that spared England and the Netherlands from absorption into the Spanish empire.
events.dareDescription: Imperial rhetoric could still frame defeat as trial, storm, and honorable endurance.
events.significance: Don Quixote's repeated falls echo a larger culture learning that confident scripts do not guarantee victory.

events.title: American silver and the Price Revolution
events.truthDescription: Sixteenth-century American silver aggravated inflation in Spain, and much treasure went to court display, imports, armies, and creditors rather than productive investment.
events.dareDescription: The empire could look rich in metals and poor in stability at the same time: a perfect backdrop for a hidalgo rich in fantasy and poor in cash.
events.significance: The novel's inns, wages, food, debts, and battered bodies matter because the fantasy unfolds in a material economy.

events.title: Don Quixote Part I is published
events.truthDescription: The first volume was printed in Madrid by Juan de la Cuesta and appeared in January 1605 after Francisco de Robles bought the publishing rights.
events.dareDescription: The would-be knight immediately became a public figure. The world began reading the man who had lost himself by reading.
events.significance: Part II will turn this publication into plot: characters inside the fiction know Part I exists.

events.title: The expulsion of the Moriscos
events.truthDescription: Philip III's government ordered the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609; by 1614 roughly 275,000 had been forced to leave Spain, according to Britannica.
events.dareDescription: Official language framed the policy as purification and security, but the human cost kept returning through exile, loss, and divided belonging.
events.significance: Part II includes Ricote, Sancho's Morisco neighbor, making a current political trauma part of the novel's moral landscape.

events.title: The false sequel appears
events.truthDescription: An unauthorized continuation of Don Quixote appeared under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda before Cervantes's own Part II.
events.dareDescription: Even the hero's identity becomes contested territory: other writers try to seize the adventure and redirect the legend.
events.significance: Cervantes answers the false sequel inside Part II, making authorship, reputation, and readerly ownership part of the story.

events.title: Don Quixote Part II is published
events.truthDescription: The second volume appeared in 1615, ten years after Part I. The Library of Congress notes the second volume's appearance a decade after the first.
events.dareDescription: The sequel lets Don Quixote walk through a world that has already read him, turning fame itself into an enchantment.
events.significance: Part II makes the novel astonishingly modern: characters discuss the book they are inside, and the boundary between life and print keeps collapsing.

events.title: Cervantes dies in Madrid
events.truthDescription: Cervantes died in Madrid in April 1616, the year after Part II appeared.
events.dareDescription: The author exits, but the knight and squire keep riding through editions, translations, art, theater, and classrooms.
events.significance: The afterlife of Don Quixote is part of the point: a book about being possessed by books became one of the most durable books in world literature.
